Content: Insights through dashboards   
 Dashboards in the Z Data Analytics Platform are a collection of visualizations that show different views of related data. A dashboard helps you get a complete picture of your data activity. 
 Dashboards provide a graphical interface so that you can monitor, explore, and gain insights from your data effectively. Whether you are tracking key performance indicators, analyzing trends, or monitoring operational metrics, dashboards offer a centralized view to facilitate data-driven decision-making. 
 Using dashboards in the Z Data Analytics Platform, you can create dynamic charts, graphs, and other visualizations that update in real-time as your data changes. You can tailor your dashboards to fit specific needs by arranging panels, applying filters, and setting time ranges. You can also use the search bar and filters to drill down into your data to uncover detailed insights and trends. If needed, you can also share your dashboards with team members and stakeholders. 
 To access the  Dashboards  page, click the Navigation icon   to open the  Navigation  panel, and then select  Z Data Analytics Platform  >  Dashboards .
Insights through dashboards
Dashboards list view    The  Dashboards  page displays a list of all the dashboards that are available to your ID in the Z Data Analytics Platform. The list view helps you to easily navigate and manage your dashboard collection. 
 The list view displays the dashboard details in a tabular format. The following table headers are displayed as a default feature:   
 Title  - Displays the name of the dashboard. 
 
 Type  - Indicates the category or type of dashboard. 
 
 Description  - Provides a brief summary or explanation, if any, of the dashboard's purpose. 
 
 Last updated  - Displays the date and time when the dashboard was last modified. 
 
 Actions  - Provides options to interact with or manage the dashboard, such as editing or deleting it. 
     You can create a new dashboard by clicking  Create Dashboard , which opens an interface to define and customize a new dashboard. It helps you to select the relevant visualizations, add titles and descriptions, choose the layout that best suits your needs, and so on. After the new dashboard is created, it is added to your dashboard list, where you can manage it further. 
 If you want to modify an existing dashboard, click its name in the list. It opens the dashboard in the edit mode, where you can adjust its contents, layout, settings, and so on. Also, the  Search  bar of the list provides a quick way to find specific dashboards by their titles or keywords, helping you navigate large collections efficiently.

Generally, the term  data store  refers to an IMS system. More precisely, however, the term data store represents the OTMA target member    (tmember) connection to an IMS system. For example, an    instance of  IMS Connect  can    have multiple data store definitions for the same IMS    system, in which case each data store represents a different OTMA tmember connection to that IMS system. 
 IMS Connect  also    supports callout requests from IMS application programs    running in IMS dependent regions. IMS application programs issue callout requests to request data or services    from a provider that is external to the IMS installation.    During a callout request, IMS acts as a client and the    external provider is the server. 
       
 IMS Connect client support  As a TCP/IP server and a message router for IMS,       IMS Connect provides access to IMS TM, IMS DB, and the CSL     Operations Manager (OM). The client support provided by IMS     Connect differs, depending on which type of access the IMS     Connect client needs. 
 
 IMS Connect support for ISC TCP/IP communications  IMS Connect manages the TCP/IP connections and protocols for IMS when Intersystem Communication (ISC) parallel sessions use TCP/IP to link to  IBM 								CICS Transaction Server for z/OS . 
 
 IMS Connect support for IMS-to-IMS TCP/IP communications  IMS Connect manages the TCP/IP connections and protocols for IMS systems that communicate with each other across a TCP/IP network. 
 
 Overview of IMS Connect XML Conversion Support  For certain IMS Connect clients, IMS Connect can convert the XML data contained in an input message into the data structures used by IMS application programs written in either COBOL or PL/I. The data in the corresponding output message is also converted from programming language of the IMS application program back to the XML data that IMS Connect client expects.

IMS Connect and TCP/IP communications   
 The IMS Connect function of IMS provides access to both IMS DB and IMS TM from TCP/IP-enabled environments. 
 The following topics are written to help programmers, operators, and system support personnel install, configure, and administer IMS Connect to support clients that communicate with IMS by using TCP/IP connections 
         
 Overview of IMS Connect   IMS Connect  provides   high performance TCP/IP  communications between one or more  IMS Connect  clients and one or more IMS systems.  IMS Connect  supports both IMS DB and IMS TM   systems. 
 
 Overview of IMS Connect exit routines  IMS provides a variety of exit routines to support IMS Connect.  
 
 IMS Connect support for IMSplex and shared queues   IMS Connect  can send and receive IMS Operations Manager (OM) commands and response string messages between a TCP/IP client and the OM in an IMSplex by using the IMS Structured Call Interface (SCI). 
 
 IMS Connect security support  IMS Connect includes a variety of options for implementing and modifying the security checking performed on messages as they arrive in IMS Connect and, for IMS TM connections, as they arrive at the data store. 
 
 IMS Connect support for callout requests  IMS Connect is a required component when IMS application programs issue callout requests through OTMA to data or service providers that are external to the IMS installation. For both types of callout request, IMS Connect serves as the TCP/IP gateway between the IMS Connect client that use TCP/IP and the OTMA component of IMS. 
 
 IMS Connect XML message conversion  For some IMS Connect client application programs, IMS Connect can convert XML messages into either COBOL or PL/I, so that you do not need to modify existing IMS application programs to process messages submitted to IMS in XML.
IMS 15.6 - Communications and connections - IMS Connect and TCP/IP communications
IMS Connect message structures  TCP/IP clients using the z/OS® program call interface communicate with IMS Connect by using an IMS request message (IRM) header on each input message. The IRM header is used on input messages from IMS Connect client application programs to communicate protocol options to IMS Connect. The IRM header is mapped by the IMS Connect HWSIMSCB macro. 
 
 OTMA header fields used by IMS Connect  IMS Connect uses fields in the headers of messages sent to OTMA to communicate processing options and other information to IMS. 
 
 IMS Connect protocols  IMS Connect provides several different transaction protocols. 
 
 IMS Connect two-phase commit support  IMS Connect supports two phase-commit for both IMS TM transactions and IMS DB database requests. 
 
 Unicode considerations for IMS Connect  IMS Connect support for Unicode allows Unicode data to be sent to and from an IMS Connect client application. In certain circumstances, IMS Connect translates the Unicode data. 
 
 TCP/IP settings for IMS Connect  You can choose different TCP/IP values to maximize your environment settings for IMS Connect.

Content: The shared daemon   Note: The current documentation of the shared daemon is valid only for DBB 2.0.2 and later.  If you are using DBB 2.0.1 or earlier, refer to the  DBB 2.0.1 PDF  or the  DBB 2.0.0 PDF           for the shared daemon documentation. 
 Starting from DBB 2.0.2, the shared daemon configuration includes additional security mechanisms and queuing enhancements for deployment to a development LPAR. The shared daemon can be used by multiple users. It must be started before any user           tries to start a build that uses the shared daemon. 
 For information about installing and configuring the shared daemon including the RACF security definitions that need to be implemented, see  Configuring the shared and personal daemons .
The shared daemon
Benefits of using a shared daemon    In a build environment that does not include a shared daemon, a JVM starts each time a user build is requested. The JVM stops when the user build completes and starts again when another user build starts to run. So total resource utilization             can get high. 
 In a build environment that includes a shared daemon, a specified number of JVMs is configured. Regardless of the number of DBB user builds that are requested, only the specified number of JVMs is started. The build daemon handles all the incoming             user build requests, sending each request to an available JVM. If all the JVMs are busy, the daemon sends the build requests that are not processed immediately to a queue and displays the position of the build request execution in the queue.             This position moves up as the build execution carries on. 
 The shared daemon is focused on the following areas: 
   Performance.  DBB user build requests are processed more efficiently thanks to the following mechanisms:                  The processor usage from starting and stopping the JVMs is eliminated between builds.  The shared daemon maintains a pool of JVMs available for incoming build requests. The number of JVMs at launch is dynamic. It can be configured and                   then modified during operation. 
 A built-in Groovy script caching is provided for every Groovy script execution. The result of each execution is cached to accelerate the next executions. 
   
 Scalability.  With the automatic queuing of the build executions, dozens or hundreds of users can share a few JVMs. The administrator can define a maximum number of requests per queue and a maximum number of requests per user ID per queue. 
 Security.  Security is ensured thanks to the following mechanisms:                  The shared daemon includes several security mechanisms and checks to validate which user ID can use the build daemon and what functions it can execute.

Running the shared daemon    Note : Before you can run the shared daemon a number of RACF security definitions need to implemented. For more information, see  Security definitions for the shared daemon . 
 You can run the shared daemon by using any of the following methods: 
   Launching the shared daemon as a started task by using the  BGZSDSTC.jcl  JCL provided by DBB.   Note:  Ensure the following requirements are met for the user that launches the shared daemon started task. These requirements are necessary for JVM initialization:                  OMVS home directory is defined. 
 UNIX home directory is specified and not blank (defined in the RACF OMVS profile):                      The directory must be specified as a full path name. 
 The directory must exist. 
 The directory must be part of a file system that is mounted and accessible to the user. 
   
   
 Calling the shared daemon directly. You can see the usage by entering the following command: $DBB_HOME/lib/sdaemon -h
   
 Using the  startdaemon.sh  script configured earlier in  Configuring the shared and personal daemons . 
   Note:  The  JAVA_HOME  environment variable determines the Java™ version that is used to run the daemon. It defaults to the Java z/OS® UNIX installation directories if it is not set. 
   Issuing a command     To issue a command to the shared daemon, you must use the daemon client. The client can be accessed by using  groovyz  or calling the client directly ( /usr/lpp/IBM/dbb/lib/sclient -h ). 
 The following examples for using the shared daemon assume that you are using host 127.0.0.1 and port 8080. The actual host and port you use depends on your setup. 
 Note: 
   Use fully qualified file names when needed as an argument. 
 When issuing a command through the  groovyz  shell script,  DBB_DAEMON_HOST  and  DBB_DAEMON_PORT  are required.
The shared daemon
Note: 
   Use fully qualified file names when needed as an argument. 
 When issuing a command through the  groovyz  shell script,  DBB_DAEMON_HOST  and  DBB_DAEMON_PORT  are required. 
 To use with User Build, add the  -DBB_DAEMON_HOST {your server host}  and  -DBB_DAEMON_PORT {your daemon port}  options under the additional parameters section. 
     Executing using the groovyz process definition     The groovyz process definition executes a Groovy script on the daemon. The groovy script must be the first parameter following the process definition name. Any subsequent arguments or options are passed directly to the executed Groovy script. 
 Examples 
   groovyz -DBB_DAEMON_HOST 127.0.0.1 -DBB_DAEMON_PORT 8080 /u/example/build.groovy 
 sclient 127.0.0.1 8080 groovyz /u/example/build.groovy 
       Executing using the dbb process definition     The dbb process definition, added in version 3.0.1, is used to execute the DBB command line interface. Its  command syntax  is the same as when it is executed through the  dbb  shell script including                 support for user sessions. However, as starting a session is interactive, user sessions cannot be started through this interface. 
 The zBuilder can also be executed by using this process definition. 
 Examples 
   sclient 127.0.0.1 8080 dbb list collections MortgageApplication 
 sclient 127.0.0.1 8080 dbb build full 
   By default, the Groovyz shell script cannot call the dbb process definition. To do so, you must replace the Groovyz process definition passed to the client with  dbb . 
 IE:
 #daemon 
...
 $DBB_HOME /lib/sclient  $DBB_DAEMON_HOST   $DBB_DAEMON_PORT  dbb  " $@ " 
     groovyz -DBB_DAEMON_HOST 127.0.0.1 -DBB_DAEMON_PORT 8080 build full 
         Managing processes     The daemon is a process coordinator that enables you to add and remove JVM processes. 
 For example, if more JVMs are needed, you can add another JVM process with the following command: 
 sclient 127.0.0.1 8080 groovyz add

Thought: I have retrieved relevant documents and no further retrieval is required for this user query.  
Answer: DBB（Dependency Based Build）の共有デーモンを設定する手順は以下の通りです。

1. **前提条件の確認**  
   - DBB 2.0.2 以降を使用していること（それ以前は別の PDF を参照）。  
   - RACF のセキュリティ定義がすべて設定済みであること。必要な RACF コマンドは `BGZSDRAC.jcl` にサンプルが用意されています。  

2. **サンプル JCL とスクリプトの取得**  
   - **`BGZSDSTC.jcl`** – 共有デーモンを開始する JCL。`CNFG` パラメータに `startdaemon.sh` が置かれているディレクトリの親ディレクトリを設定。  
   - **`startdaemon.sh`** – デーモン起動スクリプト。以下を編集します。  
     - `HOSTNAME` と `PORT`（IP アドレス形式）を環境に合わせて変更。  
     - `PD_FILE`（`process_definitions.xml` の場所）を必要に応じて変更。  
     - `DBB_HOME` が未設定の場合は `DBB_HOME_DEFAULT` に DBB のインストールパスを設定。  
   - **`BGZSDSTP.jcl`** – 共有デーモンを停止する JCL。`CNFG` に `stopdaemon.sh` があるディレクトリの親ディレクトリを設定。  
   - **`stopdaemon.sh`** – 停止スクリプト。`DBB_HOME` をインストールディレクトリに合わせて変更し、必要なら `HOSTNAME` と `PORT` も更新。  

3. **RACF セキュリティ定義の適用**  
   - `BGZSDRAC.jcl` に記載された RACF コマンドを実行し、デーモン使用者の認可やアクセス権を設定します。  
   - これにより、どのユーザーがデーモンに接続できるか、どの機能を実行できるかが制御されます。  

4. **デーモンの起動**  
   - `BGZSDSTC.jcl` を **STARTED TASK** としてサブミットします。  
   - 起動後、JVM プールが作成され、ユーザーからのビルド要求はこのプール内の JVM に割り当てられます。  

5. **クライアントからの接続**  
   - ビルド実行時に `-DBB_DAEMON_HOST <host>` と `-DBB_DAEMON_PORT <port>` をビルドパラメータに追加します。  
   - 例: `groovyz -DBB_DAEMON_HOST 127.0.0.1 -DBB_DAEMON_PORT 8080 /u/example/build.groovy`  
   - `sclient` コマンドでも同様にホストとポートを指定してデーモンにコマンドを送れます。  

6. **キューとスケーラビリティの設定（任意）**  
   - デーモンは同時実行 JVM の数をプールサイズとして設定できます。  
   - キューの最大リクエスト数やユーザーごとの上限は `process_definitions.xml` で調整可能です。  

7. **停止手順**  
   - `BGZSDSTP.jcl` をサブミットして `stopdaemon.sh` を実行し、デーモンと JVM プールを安全に終了させます。  

**ポイントまとめ**  
- 必ず RACF 定義を先に行い、デーモン起動ユーザーが正しい OMVS ホームディレクトリを持つことを確認。  
- `startdaemon.sh` と `stopdaemon.sh` の `HOSTNAME`/`PORT` を環境に合わせて設定。  
- ビルド実行時に `DBB_DAEMON_HOST` と `DBB_DAEMON_PORT` を指定し、デーモン経由でビルドを走らせる。  

これらの手順に従えば、DBB の共有デーモンを正しく構成し、ビルドのパフォーマンスとスケーラビリティを向上させることができます。

The following section provides some guidance to consider when breaking down a monolithic codebase to achieve this kind of setup.
Planning repository layouts and scopes
Guidelines for Git repository scope and structure      The guidelines in this section can be used when considering how to cluster your codebase into Git repositories in a way that makes sense and encourages a streamlined workflow for your organization. There are several factors to balance when scoping repositories, including the following: 
   Access control    Consider who (or which teams) need access to which files. Read/write, read-only, and restricted permissions need to be preserved, and this can be achieved by separating the files into different Git repositories and then managing access accordingly through your Git provider. 
   
 Functional areas of the code    In your current system, if different teams work on different components of your application, it might make sense to make boundaries based on that. An individual can be part of one or several teams. 
   
 Decoupling    Consider decoupling applications where it makes sense to do so. This allows different functional areas to have separate release cycles, which can help promote more agility in the overall organization. 
   
 Interfaces    When scoping for Git repository layouts, consider if or how changes performed by a team in one repository might impact other teams. In other words, within a team, if a developer on that team makes a breaking change to their repository (for example, to the application's private implementation), they can just work with their team to fix it. However, if a developer makes breaking changes impacting another team (for example, to the application's public interface), then resolving it can become more complicated.

 Working with a distributed version control system like Git also means that when planning the SCM layout, one factor to consider is size. Generally, you want to avoid doing something like migrating the entire codebase of a large application into one repository. 
 Large repositories can be cumbersome for a variety of reasons (although there are organizations that successfully manage their large codebases in so-called  monorepos ). Visualizing the SCM layout      Traditionally, mainframe applications are often seen as a monolith, but as mentioned previously, it is generally not preferable to have all of your codebase in one giant repository. To begin thinking about how to separate an application "monolith" into different repositories and designing your SCM layout, you can start to think about boundaries within your application, which are formed by things such as responsibilities and ownership. 
 To use an analogy, you can think of the application like a large capital city. On the surface, it might seem like this city is one big entity - a big monolith. However, upon closer inspection, the city is broken up into districts. And while each district has its own workings (for example, each district has its own school system), all of these districts are connected by a broader infrastructure in a controlled way. There might be public transport, such as a metro or buses, which run on predefined paths and schedules. We can think of this transport infrastructure like the data flowing between application boundaries within a larger system. 
 In a similar sense, the districts within the city could be likened to groupings of related files and programs, which can be formed into their own smaller applications (in a loose sense of the term) with data flowing between them.

Content: Planning repository layouts and scopes     Because the traditionally large and monolithic nature of enterprise applications can slow down development both at the organizational level and the individual developer level, many enterprises take the migration to Git as an opportunity to examine how they can break their monolithic applications down into more agile functional Git repositories. The repository layout in the source code management (SCM) component of the continuous integration/continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipeline affects other pipeline components in several ways: 
   Repository layout affects the developer experience, as it impacts the level of isolation for development activities - in other words, how much of your development can happen independently of code or components managed in other repositories. 
 The scope of the build is typically defined by what is included inside a repository versus outside of it. For shared resources such as copybooks, other repositories might need to be pulled in. 
 The scope of the package sent to the artifact repository will depend on the outputs produced by the build step.
Planning repository layouts and scopes
Basic components in a Git SCM layout      At a high level, the Git SCM can be thought of in two components: the central Git provider, which is the source from which developers will be pulling code from and pushing code to when they do their development work, and the clone on the developer workstation. 
 Within the central Git provider, there can be multiple organizations: 
   Each organization can have multiple repositories inside it. 
 In turn, each repository can have multiple branches (or versions) of the code in the repository. 
 Branches enable updates to be isolated within a branch until they are ready to be included in other branches. This allows each developer to focus on their development task on a dedicated branch, only needing to worry about upstream and downstream impacts when they are ready to integrate those with their work. By convention, there is one branch that contains the latest, greatest, and most up-to-date agreed state of the code - this is conventionally known as  main . Other branches can exist that represent a past state of the code or new changes that are not yet ready to be included in  main .    Branching in Git is lightweight both in storage space and time - no replication of the entire set of files is required to make a new branch; rather, it is a  copy-on-update  scheme that only requires the storage of the differences in files. 
   
   On the developer's workstation, the developer will have however many repositories they have decided to clone down onto their local computer to work with. By default, the clone of the repo from the server is an entire copy of the repo which, for example, includes the same history of changes and all the same branches that exist on the server. When working on changes, the developer will switch their working tree to be the contents of a particular branch.

Answer: アプリケーションリポジトリをスコープする際に考慮すべき主な要因は以下のとおりです。

1. **アクセス制御**  
   - どのチーム・ユーザーがリポジトリ内のどのファイルに対して読み取り・書き込み権限を持つかを明確にし、権限管理をリポジトリ単位で行えるようにします。

2. **機能領域（Functional Areas）**  
   - アプリケーションの機能やコンポーネントごとにチームが分かれている場合、その境界に合わせてリポジトリを分割すると、所有権と変更管理がしやすくなります。

3. **結合度（Decoupling）**  
   - 可能な限り疎結合に設計し、異なるリポジトリ間で独立したリリースサイクルを実現します。これにより、あるリポジトリの変更が他に波及するリスクを低減できます。

4. **インターフェース**  
   - 公開インターフェース（例：コピー帳、API 定義、データ構造）への変更が他チームに与える影響を評価し、インターフェースの変更は慎重に管理します。  
   - 変更が内部実装に留まる場合はリポジトリ内で完結させ、公開インターフェースに影響する場合は別リポジトリや明確なバージョニングで管理します。

5. **サイズとパフォーマンス**  
   - 大規模リポジトリはクローンやビルドに時間がかかるため、適切な粒度で分割し、必要なコードだけを取得できるようにします。  
   - ただし、パフォーマンスは唯一の決定要因ではなく、上記の組織的・機能的要因とバランスを取ります。

6. **ビルド・パッケージングスコープ**  
   - ビルドに含める対象（コピー帳、共通ライブラリなど）をリポジトリ境界で決め、ビルド成果物のサイズと依存関係を管理しやすくします。

7. **ナビゲーションと内部構造**  
   - フォルダー構成を機能やアーキテクチャに合わせて整理し、開発者がコードベースを容易に探索できるようにします。例として、`zos/src` 配下に言語別や機能別のディレクトリを設け、`interfaces` フォルダーで他アプリケーションへの公開インターフェースを管理します。

8. **変更範囲（Change Scope）**  
   - 1 つの変更リクエストが複数リポジトリに跨らないように設計し、レビュー・承認プロセスをシンプルに保ちます。

これらの要因を総合的に評価し、組織の開発フロー、チーム構成、リリースサイクルに最適なリポジトリスコープを決定してください。

Content: Security considerations   
 ADDI Local Analysis  supports only  https  connections while communicating with the browser. The  ADDI Local Analysis  container is configured with a self-signed certificate in order for you to get started quickly. You will get a security warning message the first time you open the  ADDI Local Analysis  UI on your browser. You need to accept the risk to continue. 
 If you are not using  ADDI Local Analysis  for trial or demonstration purposes, replace the self-signed certificate with a certificate that belongs to your company or yourself. 
 To avoid the security warning message, consider generating and using a signed certificate. You have two options to install your certificate.   Replacing a self-signed certificate that is provided inside the container with your certificate in the default location 
 Configuring  ADDI Local Analysis  to look for your certificate in the location that you prefer 
     

Replacing a provided self-signed certificate with your certificate in the default location  
 Complete the following steps to replace a self-signed certificate that is provided inside the  ADDI Local Analysis  container with your company certificate or your own certificate.   Put your key-value pairs (certificate and its corresponding key files) in the location where you mount the folder with the  ADDI Local Analysis  container. 
 Copy both files to  /home/wazi/ui/api/dist/certificates  directory. cp / <path> / <container-shared-directory> / <certificate-file>  /home/wazi/ui/api/dist/certificates/ <certificate-file> 
cp / <path> / <container-shared-directory> / <key-file>  /home/wazi/ui/api/dist/certificates/ <key-file>
Security considerations
Configuring ADDI Local Analysis to use your certificate from a different location  
 By default, IBM®  ADDI Local Analysis  stores the certificate and its corresponding key in the  /home/wazi/ui/api/dist/certificates  directory. If you would like to place your certificate in a different location, you can perform one of the methods below. 
 You have two methods to configure  ADDI Local Analysis  to use a certificate from a different location besides the default location. 
 
 Method 1 : Adding the key-value pairs directly when running the  ADDI Local Analysis  container.   Transfer your certificate and key files into the  ADDI Local Analysis  container in the location where you want to place your files. 
 Run the  ADDI Local Analysis  container with the following command. docker run -it -p 5000:5000 -p 4680:4680 -e SSL_CERTIFICATE_LOCATION=<path-to-certificates> -e SSL_KEY_LOCATION=<path-to-certificates> --name <container-name> addilocal:<tag> Replace the following information:   <path-to-certificates>   Replace it with the path where you store the certificate and its corresponding key file. 
 
 <container-name>     Replace it with a container name of your choice.

Score: 0.06570445001125336
Content: Key Store Policy     A Key Store Policy defines rules for how encrypted key tokens stored in a CKDS or PKDS can be accessed and used. A Key Store Policy is collectively defined by a number of separate controls that each specify a particular rule. Most of the Key Store Policy controls work in conjunction with profiles in the CSFKEYS class and enable you to:   Specify how ICSF should respond when a key token is passed to a callable service instead of a key label (which is needed to perform a SAF authorization check). 
 Determine if applications should be prevented from creating a new key record (with a new key label) for a token that is already stored in the CKDS or PKDS (in a key record with a different key label). 
 Specify if READ access authority is sufficient to create, write to, or delete a key label, or if a higher level of access authority should be required for these actions. 
 Specify if READ access authority to an AES or DES key is sufficient to export the key (move it from encryption under a master key to encryption under an RSA key), or if UPDATE authority should be required for this action. 
 Place restrictions on how keys can be used. You can:   Restrict a particular AES or DES key from being exported, or allow it to be exported only by certain RSA keys (or only by RSA keys bound to identities in certain key certificates). 
 Restrict certain RSA keys from being used in secure export and import operations, or from being used in handshake operations. 
   
 Allows archived records in the CKDS and PKDS to be used by applications. 
 Allows archived object records in the TKDS to be used by applications. 
 Specify if CSFKEYS  private-key name  checking should be done on PKA private ECC tokens with a  private-key name  in the associated data section of the token. Private-key name checking is done for both key tokens and key labels.
Key Store Policy
Each Key Store Policy control is a resource in the XFACILIT class, and can be enabled by creating a profile for the resource using the RDEFINE command. Similarly, you can disable a control by deleting its profile using the RDELETE command.   Certain controls, when enabled, will  activate  Key Store Policy for either the CKDS or PKDS. When Key Store Policy is  activated , ICSF will identify the key label or labels associated with each key token in the key store. This information is needed, for example, in order to carry out SAF authorization checks against RACF profiles (which are based on key labels) when a key token is passed to a callable service, or to ensure an application does not store a duplicate token (a token that is already stored, but associated with a different key label) in the key store. In addition to the controls that activate Key Store Policy, other controls that do not themselves activate Key Store Policy may still require, or to a lesser degree rely upon, an active Key Store Policy and its key token/label associations. The following table outlines the Key Store Policy controls that are available. This table also highlights the controls that activate Key Store Policy for a CKDS or PKDS, as well as the dependencies the other controls have on Key Store Policy being active. Be aware that Key Store Policy is activated separately for a CKDS and a PKDS. 
       
 Defining a Key Store Policy   
 
 Enabling access authority checking for key tokens   
 
 Determining access to tokens not stored in the CKDS or PKDS   
 
 Enabling duplicate key label checking   
 
 Enabling use of archived KDS records   
 
 Increasing the level of authority needed to modify key labels   
 
 Increasing the level of authority required to export symmetric keys   
 
 Controlling how cryptographic keys can be used

ADDI（Application Discovery and Delivery Intelligence）で使用するキーストアには、以下の要件があります。

1. **物理的にクライアント側に配置**  
   - IBM ADDI Analyze Client がインストールされているマシンに、サーバー側で使用しているキーストアをコピーして配置する必要があります。  
   - キーストアのパスは `eclipse.ini`（または `developer_for_zos.ini`）の `-vmargs` セクションに `-Dclient.ssl.keyStore=` で指定します。

2. **サポートされるファイル形式**  
   - キーストアは次の拡張子のいずれかであれば使用可能です。  
     `.p12`、`.jks`、`.keystore`、`.pfx`、`.ks`

3. **パスワードの設定**  
   - キーストアのパスワードは `-Dclient.ssl.keyStorePass=` で指定します。  
   - 同様に、トラストストア（`-Dclient.ssl.trustStore=`）とそのパスワード（`-Dclient.ssl.trustStorePass=`）も設定します。

4. **サーバーが証明書を使用しない場合の対策**  
   - サーバーが証明書を持たないが、バックエンドのリレーショナルデータベースが証明書を使用している場合は、次を実施します。  
     - 各クライアントマシンにデータベースサーバーの証明書を「Trusted Root Certification Authority」にインポート。  
     - サーバー側の自己署名キーストア（`keystore.p12`）をクライアントにコピーし、`-Djavax.net.ssl.trustStore=` と `-Djavax.net.ssl.trustStorePassword=` で参照させる。

5. **設定例（eclipse.ini の抜粋）**  

   ```text
   -Dclient.ssl.keyStore=/path/to/server/keystore
   -Dclient.ssl.keyStorePass=yourPassword
   -Dclient.ssl.trustStore=/path/to/server/keystore
   -Dclient.ssl.trustStorePass=yourPassword
   ```

以上が、ADDI が必要とするキーストアの主な要件です。

Content: Options for migrating databases to use  FARF6  pool file addresses   
 You can migrate your existing databases to use  FARF6  pool file addresses in stages. 
 FARF6  pools into a database, you must enable the  FARF6  migration switch. Turn on the  FARF6  migration switch before you start any  FARF6  migration activity. All  z/TPFDF  databases that use  FARF6  addresses must also have 8-byte file address headers. You can migrate to 8-byte file address headers before or at the same time that you introduce  FARF6  pools into a database. When you introduce  FARF6  file addresses in the database, you can choose to allow  FARF6  to be used in overflow records only, or in both overflow and prime records. All detail files that have  FARF6  pool prime records also must be referenced by an 8-byte field in any corresponding index files. The index references can be migrated before or at the same time that you introduce  FARF6  prime records into a database. 
 When you migrate a database to  FARF6 , you can choose to perform migration operations on one, some, or all files within the database at a time. Within each file, you can choose to perform migration operations on one, some, or all subfiles. 
 There are many combinations of migration approaches that you can choose to take. For example, you can choose one of the following approaches:   Migrate headers in all subfiles for a file and then use  FARF6  addresses only for new overflow pools. 
 Migrate headers in all subfiles for a file and use a  CRUISE  pack operation to convert existing overflow pools to  FARF6 . 
 Migrate index references in a database and use  FARF6  addresses for overflow pools and new prime blocks. 
 Migrate the entire database to use  FARF6  pools.
Options for migrating databases to use FARF6 pool file addresses
Migrate index references in a database and use  FARF6  addresses for overflow pools and new prime blocks. 
 Migrate the entire database to use  FARF6  pools. 
     The first two of these approaches have the smallest potential impact to a database and work well for databases that have a relatively large number of overflow pools. Users that don't have many overflows in their database and need or want to use  FARF6  addresses in prime pool files need to migrate the index file references as well. Migrating one entity at a time (such as headers, then index references, and then packing to get  FARF6  addresses) allows you to more easily validate the results. However, depending on the number and size of the databases to be migrated, migrating one entity at a time can potentially be a resource-consuming approach. 
 The topics in this section provide more information about the staging options for migrating to  FARF6  file addresses and for falling back to FARF3, FARF4, or FARF5 file addresses.     8-byte file address headers for FARF6 
 FARF6 pool migration for overflow blocks 
 FARF6 pool migration for prime and overflow blocks 
 FARF6 pool migration for selected files or subfiles 
 Fallback from FARF6 pools 
     For information about the tasks necessary to complete these stages, see  Migrating to FARF6 file addresses . 
 
 Notes:     Before you begin to migrate your applications to  FARF6 , you must install  FARF6  support. For more information, see  Prepare the z/TPFDF product and applications for FARF6 . 
 The  z/TPFDF product  provides an automatic migration capability by using an existing  CRUISE  tool that can automatically reformat a database to be compatible with  FARF6  and then migrate the data. The  z/TPFDF product  does not provide a tool to dynamically change the FARF format that a subfile uses. 
           
 FARF6 pool migration for overflow blocks  For existing databases, you can choose to convert only overflow blocks to  FARF6  file addresses.
Options for migrating databases to use FARF6 pool file addresses
FARF6 pool migration for overflow blocks  For existing databases, you can choose to convert only overflow blocks to  FARF6  file addresses. 
 
 FARF6 pool migration for prime and overflow blocks  If the number of subfiles that your applications support might exceed the number of FARF3, FARF4, or FARF5 file addresses, you can convert prime blocks and overflow blocks to use  FARF6  file addresses. 
 
 FARF6 pool migration for selected files or subfiles  If only selected files or subfiles are growing rapidly, or you want migrate your databases by stages, you can convert selected files or subfiles in a file to be compatible with  FARF6  or use  FARF6  pools. 
 
 Fallback from FARF6 pools  If you turn on the migration switch to enable  FARF6  support, you cannot disable the support; however, you can fall back from  FARF6  file addresses to FARF3, FARF4, or FARF5 file addresses.

1. **事前準備**  
   - **FARF6 サポートの有効化**  
     - `ZMODE` コマンドで FARF6 移行スイッチをオンにします。これにより、z/TPFDF が FARF6 アドレス形式を認識できるようになります。

2. **アプリケーションコードの更新**  
   - 8 バイトファイルアドレスを扱えるようにプログラムを修正します。  
   - アプリケーションコードは、データベース定義が有効になる前でも更新可能です。  

3. **データベース定義（DBDEF）の移行**  
   - **FARF6 プール使用の指定**  
     - `DBDEF` マクロに `F6PRP=YES`（prime プール）や `F6OFP=YES`（overflow プール）を追加し、FARF6 プールを使用することを宣言します。  
   - **DBDEF のビルドとアクティベート**  
     - 変更した DBDEF をビルドし、`ZFCRU` 系コマンドでアクティベートします。  

4. **データの実際の移行**  
   - **CRUISE ツール（ZFCRU）を使用したキャプチャ／リストア**  
     1. データベースをオフラインにする。  
     2. `ZFCRU LOCK` で CRUISE テーブルをロックし、`ZFCRU SETUP` でキャプチャ対象のサブファイル ID を指定。  
     3. `ZFCRU UNLOCK` でロック解除し、テープ等にキャプチャ（`ZFCRU START` を 2 回実行）。  
     4. 同様に `ZFCRU LOCK/SETUP/UNLOCK` で「RESTORE‑REBUILD」モードを設定し、`ZFCRU START` を 2 回実行して新しい FARF6 プールへリストア。  
   - **段階的移行の選択肢**  
     - **オーバーフローブロックのみ**：オーバーフローブロックだけを FARF6 に変換。  
     - **プライム＋オーバーフロー**：プライムブロックも含めてすべてを FARF6 に変換。  
     - **ファイル／サブファイル単位**：対象ファイルやサブファイルを選択的に移行し、リスクを分散。  

5. **検証**  
   - `F6WARN` パラメータ（`DBDEF` マクロ）を使用して、FARF6 へ完全に移行できているかをチェック。  
   - 移行後はデータベースをオンラインにし、アプリケーションの動作確認を行います。  

6. **フォールバック（必要な場合）**  
   - 移行後に問題が発生した場合は、FARF3/FARF4/FARF5 形式へ戻すことが可能です（「Falling back an existing pool database」参照）。ただし、FARF6 スイッチは無効化できない点に注意してください。

- 移行は「FARF6 スイッチ有効化 → 8 バイトヘッダー導入 → アプリ更新 → DBDEF 更新 → CRUISE によるデータキャプチャ/リストア」の流れで実施。  
- 段階的に移行できるので、影響範囲を限定しながらテストを行うことが推奨されます。  
- 移行完了後は `F6PRP=YES, F6OFP=YES, F6SHORT=YES` を残したまま運用を続けます。

Content: Generating Java classes and methods using incremental generation or bulk generation approach
Generating Java methods using bulk generation approach    If you selected the  Bulk generation  option in  Step 4 , then the application generates all required  Java  classes and methods for the selected  COBOL  program. 
 A message box appears, indicating the progress of method generation in percentage. While generating  Java  methods using bulk generation approach, the application continues the method generation in the background while you can use the editor to continue working on other  Java  or  COBOL  files. 
 You can click  Cancel  on the message box at any time during the generation process. Although the application stops creating new methods, it completes generating any methods that are already in progress. 
 After completing  Java  class and method generation, the following message is displayed:  Generating  Java  for  COBOL  program < COBOL  program name> complete. 
 Compared to the  Incremental generation  approach,  Bulk generation  class generation takes longer as all  Java  classes and methods are generated at once. 
 You can view a list of all generated  Java  files in the  watsonx Code Assistant for Z  view. Observe that the icon preceding the  Java  files indicate that method generation is completed. 
 
 Note:  Bulk method generation is single-threaded, translating one program at a time to be better synced with the outline view provided by the  Red Hat  extension.
Generating Java classes and methods using incremental generation or bulk generation approach
Usage-based generation of utility methods    When  COBOL  paragraphs are transformed to  Java , by default every generated  Java  class includes utility methods, regardless of usage. This results in high code emolument per class, slower compile and test cycles, and cluttered codebase. Some of these generated methods are not called by the actual business logic. 
 The usage-based generation approach generates only the necessary utility methods in  Java  classes based on actual usage. This reduces unnecessary boilerplate by including methods only when they are referenced in the program logic, enabling a demand-driven code generation strategy results in more efficient output. The reduced code size results in cleaner code bases, lowering cognitive load on developers and improving performance. 
   2.6.10+ 
 

Renaming Java variables, classes, serializer classes and methods    When  COBOL  programs are transformed to  Java , you can edit the names of  Java  variables, classes, serializer classes and methods created during transformation. When you rename a variable, class, serializer class or method, all occurrences of the variable, class, serializer class or method within the transformed  Java  code are automatically renamed. 
 This feature can be enabled by configuring the  edit_java_class_names  parameter of the  wcaz-settings.yaml  settings file.  
 Note:  The  wcaz-settings.yaml  settings file is located in the  transform  folder of the  .wca4z  tree.     Here is a sample  wcaz-settings.yaml  settings file. 
 transform_settings:
      # Database connectivity type options: "JDBC" or "SQLJ"
      Database_connectivity: "JDBC"

      # Lombok library options: "Enabled" or "Disabled"
      lombok_library: "Enabled"

 Note:   IBM watsonx Code Assistant for Z  does not support multi-root workspace with transform.   There are several approaches to transform  COBOL  to Java: 
   
 Generating Java logic without generating Java classes : This approach allows you to directly transform selected  COBOL  programs to Java methods and attach these methods to predefined classes. 
 
 Generating Java methods for the initial Java classes using incremental generation approach : This approach allows you to gradually generate  Java  classes and methods based on your requirements. 
 
 Generating Java methods using bulk generation approach : In this approach, all  Java  classes and methods are generated at once. While this approach may be time effective, it is difficult to understand the relationship between the various methods and classes generated, or to fix errors.

Content: DBDEL: Delete one or more logical records
If you delete all the LRECs from a pool subfile by using the  NOKEY  parameter or with no keys active, the DBDEL macro releases the overflow blocks and marks the prime block for release during close processing. For more information about processing details, see the  RELFC  parameter description in  DBCLS: Close a subfile . Note that if you delete all the LRECs from a pool subfile, and either add an LREC or issue a DBUHLD macro before you close the subfile, the prime block is no longer marked for release. 
 For  B + Tree  files, if no keys are specified, the DBDEL macro with the  ALL  parameter releases the  B + Tree  node blocks as well as the data blocks. 
     
 INITIALISE     Initializes a subfile if you are using the  NOKEY  parameter or no keys are active. Delete processing immediately releases all overflow blocks and initializes the header in the prime block, which will not be marked for release. 
 If the subfile is a remote subfile, the subfile is still considered a remote subfile and an empty document is maintained in the remote data store. Any LRECs that are subsequently added to the subfile will be stored in the remote data store unless the subfile location is changed by an application. 
 If keys are active, or you specify this parameter with the  KEY n  parameters, this parameter is ignored. 
 You can specify this parameter as  INITIALISE  or  INITIALIZE . 
 
 DOWNWARD   Deletes all LRECs from (and including) the current LREC to the last LREC in the subfile. If you opened the subfile using   KEY n  parameters, the DBDEL macro deletes only the LRECs that match these keys. 
 UPWARD   Deletes all LRECs from (but not including) the current LREC to the first LREC in the subfile. If you opened the subfile using   KEY n  parameters, the DBDEL macro deletes only the LRECs that match these keys. 
 BEGIN   Searches from the beginning of the subfile for LRECs to delete. 
 CHKA= rcc

Content: dfrst: Restore a subfile
Programming considerations  
   The type definitions (for example,  dft_fil ,  dft_ref , and  dft_kyl ) are defined in the  c_cdfapi.h  header file. 
 If the  acc  parameter contains an address above the  2 GB bar  when the  access  parameter is set to the  DFRST_ALG  (pointer to an algorithm) option, performance can be affected. 
 Some parameters can be of different types based on the value you specify for that parameter or a related parameter. In the function format, the type of these parameters is shown as  dft_ xxx . For more information, see the description of the specific parameter for information about what type definition to use for that parameter. 
 The  dfrst  function rebuilds the  B + Tree  index for  B + Tree  files. 
 If you issue a  dfrst  function on a subfile that was opened in detac mode, changes that were made to the subfile before the  dfrst  function call cannot be rolled back by issuing a  dfcls  function with the  DFCLS_ABORT  option. However, the restored target subfile remains open in detac mode when  dfrst  processing is complete. 
 If the target subfile previously existed and was stored in a remote data store before this function was called, the target subfile is removed from that data store. 
 If you do not specify the  DFRST_FLIP  option, after  dfrst  function processing, the target subfile is stored in the same location as the source subfile, either locally on the  z/TPF system  or in the same remote data store as the source subfile. 
 If you specify the  DFRST_FLIP  option, the location of where each subfile is stored is swapped along with the data in the subfile.  
 If you specify the  DFRST_FLIP  option, you must specify the same header and file address format type for the source and destination or an error is returned. If a new pool is allocated, the pool is created using the same header and file address format as the source.
dfrst: Restore a subfile
The file addresses of the source and destination must have the same header and file address format; otherwise the result is unpredictable. If a new pool is allocated, it is created using the same header and file address format as the source. 
 For programming considerations when you use this function with  data event processing , see  z/TPFDF API programming considerations for data event processing .
dfrst: Restore a subfile
Examples

dft_fil *file_ptr;
⋮
dfrst(file_ptr, DFRST_HELD, fad);

dft_fad file_address;
⋮

[Rank 4] Title: IBM z/Transaction Processing Facility Enterprise Edition Pool use with remote subfiles
URL: 
Score: 0.09698273241519928
Content: Pool use with remote subfiles   
 When an application updates and closes a remote subfile, the existing prime block and overflow records are used to temporarily store the updated subfile data.  
 After the remote subfile asynchronous update process updates the remote subfile data in the remote data store, the process leaves the overflow records chained to the prime block so that the overflow records can be used for the next access of that subfile. 
 If the remote data store mode is set to REMOTE, the data for a remote subfile is stored only in the remote data store. As a result, the remote subfile asynchronous update process deletes the LREC data from the subfile after the process successfully updates the remote data store. The empty overflow records are left chained to the prime block so the empty overflow records can be used for the next access of that subfile. The empty overflow records are kept even if the  DELEMPTY  parameter is specified on the DBDEF macro.  
 Most of the data for large logical records (LLRs) is not stored in a chain of traditional overflow records. If a remote subfile contains LLRs, remote subfile processing gets new pool records for the LLRs whenever an application reads the remote subfile from the remote data store. In addition, after the remote subfile asynchronous update process processes the remote subfile data in the remote data store,  the process releases the pool records for the LLR data. As a result, if your remote subfiles contain LLRs, you might see increased pool usage on your   z/TPF system .
#

If you do not enter the command a second time within two minutes, the pending initialization is automatically canceled.

Content: IMS 15.6 - Database administration - Database concepts and terminology
Database concepts and terminology   
 This topic discusses the terms and concepts you need to understand to perform IMS database administration tasks. 
 To understand this topic, you must know what a DL/I call is and how to code it. You must understand function codes and Segment Search Arguments (SSAs) in DL/I calls and know what is meant when a call is referred to as qualified or unqualified (explained in  IMS 					Version 15.6 Application Programming ). 
       
 How data is stored in a database  The data in a database is grouped into a series of  database records . Each database record is composed of smaller groups of data called  segments . A segment is the smallest piece of data IMS can store. Segments, in turn, are made up of one or more  fields . 
 
 The hierarchy in a database record  A database is composed of a series of database records. Records contain segments, and the segments are arranged in a hierarchy in the database record. 
 
 Types of IMS databases  IMS allows you to define many different database types. You define the database type that best suits your application's processing requirements.  
 
 The database record  A database consists of a series of database records, and a database record consists of a series of segments.  
 
 The segment  A database record consists of one or more segments, and the segment is the smallest piece of data IMS can store.

Content: IMS 15.6 - Database administration - Format of records in the IMS catalog database
Format of records in the IMS catalog database   
 The IMS catalog database contains a unique record for each PSB and DBD defined during ACB generation. Each type of record, and each type of segment within a record, has a predefined format. 
 The catalog database segment types are grouped into four different data set groups (A - D) based on how frequently that segment type is accessed in database queries. The most frequently accessed segment types, such as the root segment type (HEADER), are located in data set group A. The least frequently accessed segment types, such as user remarks segments, are grouped in data set D. 
 Some segment types in the catalog database, such as DBDHXXX, are not currently used and are reserved for future development. The segment definitions are included in the catalog to allow for the implementation of future service and development enhancements without an unload and reload of the catalog database. 
       
 HEADER segment format  The IMS catalog HEADER segment type, also called the resource header, is the root segment type for the IMS catalog database. 
 
 DBD record segment formats  The DBD record segments in the IMS catalog are used to store information about an IMS database definition (DBD). 
 
 PSB record segment formats  The PSB record segments in the IMS catalog are used to store information about application program views and schemas of IMS databases, otherwise known as program specification blocks (PSBs) and program communication blocks (PCBs).

Content: IMS 15.6 - Database administration - How an HSAM record is stored
How an HSAM record is stored   
 Segments in an HSAM database are loaded in the order in which you present them to the load program.  
 You should present all segments within a database record in hierarchical sequence. If a sequence field has been defined for root segments, you should present database records to the load program in ascending root key sequence. 
 The following figure shows an example HSAM database.  
 Figure 1. Example HSAM database       The following figure shows how the example HSAM database shown in the preceding figure would be stored in blocks. 
 Figure 2. Example HSAM database stored in blocks       In the data set, a database record is stored in one or more consecutive blocks. You define what the block size will be. Each block is filled with segments of the database record until there is not enough space left in the block to store the next segment. When this happens, the remaining space in the block is padded with zeros and the next segment is stored in the next consecutive block. When the last segment of a database record has been stored in a block, any unused space, if sufficient, is filled with segments from the next database record. 
 In storage, an HSAM segment consists of a 2-byte prefix followed by user data. The first byte of the prefix is the segment code, which identifies the segment  type  to IMS. This number can be from 1 to 255. The segment code is assigned to the segment by IMS in ascending sequence, starting with the root segment and continuing through all dependents in hierarchical sequence. The second byte of the prefix is the delete byte. Because DLET calls cannot be used against an HSAM database, the second byte is not used.

Content: IMS 15.6 - Database administration - The segment
The segment   
 A database record consists of one or more segments, and the segment is the smallest piece of data IMS can store.  
 Here are some additional facts you need to know about segments:   
   A database record can contain a maximum of 255 segment types. The space you allocate for the database limits the number of segment occurrences. 
 You determine the length of a segment; however, a segment cannot be larger than the physical record length of the device on which it is stored. 
 The length of segments is specified by segment type. A segment type can be either variable or fixed in length. 
   Segments consist of two parts (a prefix and the data), except when using a SHSAM or SHISAM database. In SHSAM and SHISAM databases, the segment consists of only the data. In a GSAM database, segments do not exist. 
 The following figure shows the format of a fixed-length segment. 
 Figure 1. Format of fixed-length segments         The following figure shows the format of a variable-length segment. 
 Figure 2. Format of variable-length segments       IMS uses the prefix portion of the segment to  manage  the segment. The prefix portion of a segment consists of: segment code, delete byte, and in some databases, a pointer and counter area. Application programs do not  see  the prefix portion of a segment. The data portion of a segment contains your data, arranged in one or more fields. 
       
 Segment code  IMS needs a way to identify each segment type stored in a database. It uses the segment code field for this purpose.  
 
 Delete byte  When an application program deletes a segment from a database, the space it occupies might or might not be immediately available to reuse.  
 
 Pointer and counter area  The pointer and counter area exists in HDAM, PHDAM, HIDAM, and PHIDAM databases, and, in some special circumstances, HISAM databases.
IMS 15.6 - Database administration - The segment
Pointer and counter area  The pointer and counter area exists in HDAM, PHDAM, HIDAM, and PHIDAM databases, and, in some special circumstances, HISAM databases.  
 
 The data portion  The data portion of a segment contains one or more data elements. The data is processed and unlike the prefix portion of the segment, seen by an application program. 
 
 The three data portion field types  You can define three field types in the data portion of a segment: a sequence field, data fields, and for variable-length segments, a size field stating the length of the segment.

X'14'       Switched-line disconnect.   
   X'15'       Switched-line connect.   
   X'16'   IMS_V nnn _16   Sign-on/off record.  This record logs the security maintenance utility (SMU) or Resource Access Control Facility (RACF®) user sign-on and sign-off. 
   
   X'18'   IMS_V nnn _18   Extended checkpoint record.  This record logs the details and checkpoint data for an extended checkpoint. 
   
   X'20'   IMS_V nnn _20   Database open record.  This record indicates that a DL/I database was opened and describes various key characteristics of the database and its files. 
   
   X'21'   IMS_V nnn _21   Database close record.  This record indicates that a DL/I database was closed and provides several key details about the database and its files. A database open  X'20'  record was created earlier. 
   
   X'24'   IMS_V nnn _24   Database error record.  This record indicates that a DL/I database had an error. It details the program and transaction accessing the database at the time of the error, the time the error occurred, and the relative byte address (RBA) and cylinder cylinder head head record (CCHHR) details of the error. 
   
   X'25'       EEQE record.   
   X'26'       I/O toleration buffer.   
   X'27'       Database extension.   
   X'28'       Phase 1 DC record.   
   X'30'   IMS_V nnn _30   Message queue prefix changed record.  This record logs changes made to the message queue record prefix. It links directly to a previously logged message. 
   
   X'31'   IMS_V nnn _31   Message queue GU record.  This record logs the details of a message that is GU'd from the message queue to be sent to its destination. The destination may be an SMB or CNT. 
 The record is present for incoming messages that are processed by a program scheduled in a message processing region, or for outgoing messages that are sent to a network destination. In addition, the record is present for message switches.
Descriptions of record definitions
The timestamp in this record essentially represents the time that the message ceased waiting on the message queue. If the message is sent to a CNT, a type  X'36'  record follows, ultimately being followed by a type  X'33'  Free record, regardless of destination. 
   
   X'32'   IMS_V nnn _32   Message queue reject record.  This record is produced when the MSGQ rejects a message because an error occurred, presumably causing an application program abend. 
   
   X'33'   IMS_V nnn _33   Message queue DRRN free record.  This record indicates that DRRNs were freed from the message queues, the message was deleted, and the DRRNs are available for reuse. 
 This record always indicates that the message is no longer needed by IMS . 
   
   X'34'   IMS_V nnn _34   Message queue cancel record.  This record indicates that the message was canceled from the queue and that a subsequent  X'35'  Enqueue record was not produced. 
   
   X'35'   IMS_V nnn _35   Message queue enqueue record.  This record indicates that the message in the message queue (logged as a type  X'01'  or  X'03'  record) has been placed on the queue for processing. If the destination is an SMB, it is usually waiting on the input queue for the PSB to issue the Get Unique. If the destination is a CNT, it is either a message switch or an outbound message and is waiting in the output queue. 
 This record follows the logging of the message as a  X'01'  or  X'03'  record, and precedes the  X'31'  record that indicates the message has been retrieved from the queue for processing or transmission. 
 The timestamp can be carried from the preceding  X'01'  or  X'03' . Because the timestamp from this record may not reflect the real time the message arrived in the system, exercise caution when using it.

Answer: IMS データベースレコードは、IMS データベース内に格納される最小単位のデータ構造です。レコードは 1 つ以上の **セグメント** で構成され、各セグメントはさらに 1 つ以上の **フィールド**（データ要素）を持ちます。  

- **レコード (record)**  
  - データベース全体を構成するエンティティの集合体。  
  - 複数のセグメントが階層的に配置され、レコード全体が 1 つの論理的なデータ単位となります。  

- **セグメント (segment)**  
  - レコード内の最小格納単位で、IMS が管理できる最小のデータブロックです。  
  - セグメントは「プレフィックス（セグメントコード、削除バイト等）＋データ部」の構造を持ち、データ部は 1 つ以上のフィールドで構成されます。  

- **フィールド (field)**  
  - セグメント内に定義された個々のデータ項目で、実際にアプリケーションが使用する値が格納されます。  

レコードはデータベースの物理的なストレージ上では 1 つ以上の連続したブロックに格納され、ブロックサイズやデバイスの制限に応じてセグメントが順次配置されます（HSAM データベースの場合はブロック単位で格納されます）。  

要するに、IMS データベースレコードは「レコード → セグメント → フィールド」という 3 階層構造でデータを管理し、IMS が提供する高速検索・更新機能の基礎となる概念です。

Content: Filter collections by using  z/TPF support for MongoDB 
   
 A filtered collection is a logical subset or view of a collection or a subset of logical records (LRECs) of a  z/TPFDF  file. As a database administrator, you can use filtered collections to control the visibility of the data in a collection.  
 z/TPF user security  restricts access at the collection level. However, giving users access to full collections might cause a security violation when the records in those collections contain sensitive information. You can define filtered collections to better control access to data in your collections. By using filtered collections, you can expose or keep hidden LRECs by creating filtered collections based on LREC types and filtering the LRECs in the filtered collections.

Filtering records in a filtered collection    When you create a filtered collection, you can define a rule by using the <FilterRule> element in the  z/TPFDF collection descriptor  that defines access to each LREC in the collection.  
 The <FilterRule> element is a  DFDL  expression that evaluates to a Boolean value. By defining filter rules, you can limit the records that a user can access in a collection. For more information about the  DFDL  comparison expression, see  Supported DFDL v1.0 Specification . 
 The following examples illustrate two ways that you might use filter rules based on the amount of data that you are managing:    A  z/TPFDF  file contains data for a small number of different customers. For example, a particular  z/TPFDF  file might contain data for several different airlines. If the number of the airlines is small and a field in each LREC associates the LREC with each airline, you can create a filtered collection for each airline. In the filtered collection, define a  DFDL  expression to compare data in the LRECs with a fixed value to ensure that only the data of that airline is exposed.  
 A filtered collection is created for each airline, so you can use the  z/TPF user security  database to manage the access to each filtered collection.  
 For an example of how you can use filter rules for this type of situation, see  Filtering records by using fixed data . 
 
 A  z/TPFDF  file contains data for a large number of different customers. For example, a single  z/TPFDF  file might contain credit card information for every customer.  If the number of customers is large, you can create one filtered collection for all of the data. In the filtered collection, define a  DFDL  expression to compare data in the LRECs with data that is entered by the user to ensure that only the data that matches the user input is exposed.

Content: z/TPF support for MongoDB enhancements  ( APAR  PJ45541)   
 z/TPF support for MongoDB  is enhanced to provide improved usability and additional functionality. 
 

Object ID formatting enhancement    An optional attribute, idType, is added to the Collection element of the  z/TPFDF collection descriptor . This attribute controls whether to format the _id field of a  MongoDB  document in a filtered collection by using the filtered ID or the object ID. The filtered ID is a structure that includes the object ID, index name, and algorithm string. 
 In some cases, a remote  MongoDB  client might get a prime file address for a subfile from a previous query and try to open that subfile directly by using the file address in the _id field. Previously, the filtered ID was always used to locate data for filtered collections, and the object ID was always used to locate data for unfiltered collections. If you needed to query  MongoDB  data, you had to know in advance whether the data was part of a filtered or an unfiltered collection and format the _id field accordingly. 
 With this enhancement, you can control how the _id field is formatted for  MongoDB  documents in collections that are filtered on fixed data. By setting the idType attribute of the Collection element to the  ObjectID  value in the  z/TPFDF collection descriptor , you can force the  MongoDB  server to locate data and return documents by using only the object ID for the _id field. Therefore, collections that map to the same z/TPFDF subfile can use the same format for the _id field, whether the collections are filtered or not. You no longer need to know ahead of time whether the queried data is filtered or not.
z/TPF support for MongoDB enhancements (APAR PJ45541)
Configurable receive and send buffer sizes    This enhancement provides new options for you to configure the socket receive and send buffer sizes when you are defining a  z/TPF  server for  MongoDB . 
 Previously, when a  z/TPF  server for  MongoDB  was started, the socket send and receive buffer sizes used the default 32 KB buffer size. If  MongoDB  requests or responses were larger than 32 KB, the throughput might be affected because the TCP endpoint could send only 32 KB of data through the network at a time. 
 With this enhancement, you can specify the  --rbuf  and  --sbuf  options to configure the socket receive and send buffer sizes when you are defining a  z/TPF  server for  MongoDB . By increasing the buffer sizes, you can improve the throughput and reduce the response time for large  MongoDB  requests or responses.  
     For more information about  APAR   PJ45541 , see the APEDIT.

Content: z/TPF support for MongoDB   
 
 With  z/TPF support for MongoDB , remote distributed platforms can access and update data in a  z/TPF  database by using the  MongoDB Query Language .   You do not need to change  z/TPF  application code to use  z/TPF support for MongoDB .   MongoDB  is a NoSQL database and treats data as documents.  MongoDB  documents are described by using   JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) , which is an open and human- and machine-readable standard to facilitate data exchange. The  z/TPF  database is not a NoSQL database, but you can create a  JSON  document from the data in the  z/TPF  database. 
       
 Access z/TPF data by using z/TPF support for MongoDB  The  z/TPF   Internet Daemon  ( InetD ) is used to access the  z/TPF  data by using  z/TPF support for MongoDB .  z/TPF support for MongoDB  is provided only for  z/TPFDF  databases.  
 
 MongoDB terminology  Some concepts in  z/TPFDF  and  MongoDB  are similar, but the terms to refer to these concepts might be different. 
 
 z/TPFDF database definition (DBDEF) considerations   z/TPF support for MongoDB  supports only R-type  z/TPFDF  files. Some settings in the  z/TPFDF  database definitions change the behavior of  z/TPF support for MongoDB .  
 
 Add default keys by using z/TPFDF default key support  With  z/TPFDF default key support for z/TPF support for MongoDB , you can define default keys for  z/TPFDF  files in the  z/TPFDF collection descriptors  ( adbi.xml  files). 
 
 Setting up z/TPF support for MongoDB  You must define a  z/TPF  server for  MongoDB  before you can connect  MongoDB  remote clients to the  z/TPF system  by using  z/TPF support for MongoDB . 
 
 Preparing the z/TPF system for data access by using z/TPF support for MongoDB  You must prepare the  z/TPF system  before you can access  z/TPF  databases by using  z/TPF support for MongoDB .

Preparing the z/TPF system for data access by using z/TPF support for MongoDB  You must prepare the  z/TPF system  before you can access  z/TPF  databases by using  z/TPF support for MongoDB . 
 
 z/TPF support for MongoDB security  To maintain a secure environment, you must implement controls to ensure that users have access only to data that they are authorized to access.  
 
 z/TPF user security   By using  z/TPF user security , you can define  z/TPF  user IDs, passwords, and privileges to  z/TPF  data and resources. You can use  z/TPF user security  only for   z/TPF support for MongoDB  applications.  
 
 Analyze the performance of z/TPF support for MongoDB  You can use   resource usage by owner name collection  on the  z/TPF system  to collect resource usage information for the  MongoDB  applications based on the owner name. You can specify the high-level qualifier and mid-level qualifier in the  resource usage by owner name configuration file  to collect resource usage information by specific categories.  
 
 Operations and coverage considerations for z/TPF support for MongoDB  There are operational considerations to remember when you use  z/TPF support for MongoDB .  
 
 User exits for MongoDB request processing  For each  MongoDB  request,  z/TPF support for MongoDB  provides two user exits, the pre-request user exit (UMON_pre_request) and post-request user exit (UMON_post_request) for you to control pre-request and post-request processing.  
 
 Filter collections by using z/TPF support for MongoDB  A filtered collection is a logical subset or view of a collection or a subset of logical records (LRECs) of a  z/TPFDF  file. As a database administrator, you can use filtered collections to control the visibility of the data in a collection.

MongoDB の z/TPF サポートでフィルタされたコレクション（filtered collection）を定義する手順は、主に **z/TPFDF コレクション記述子（adbi.xml など）** に情報を記述することで行います。

1. **コレクション要素に filtered 属性を付与**  
   ```xml
   <tns:Collection name="CustomerService"
                   filtered="true"
                   dfdlfile="CustomerInfo.tpfdf.dfdl.xsd"
                   collectionId="C412">
   ```
   `filtered="true"` を設定すると、そのコレクションはフィルタされたコレクションとして扱われます。

2. **対象とする LREC（Logical Record）を列挙**  
   フィルタされたコレクションに含めたい LREC だけを `<tns:Lrecs>` 要素内に記述します。  
   ```xml
   <tns:Lrecs>
       <tns:Lrec name="CustomerRecord" id="70"/>
       <tns:Lrec name="ServiceRecord"  id="C0"/>
   </tns:Lrecs>
   ```
   例では `PaymentRecord`（機密情報）を除外しています。

3. **<FilterRule> 要素でレコード単位の条件を設定（任意）**  
   - **固定データでのフィルタ**：DFDL 式で固定値と比較し、特定の顧客や航空会社だけを公開。  
   - **可変データでのフィルタ**：ユーザー入力値と比較する DFDL 式を使用し、実行時に条件を決定。  
   ```xml
   <tns:FilterRule> $LREC.AirlineCode = "AA" </tns:FilterRule>
   ```

4. **_id フィールドの形式を制御（必要に応じて）**  
   `idType="ObjectID"` を `Collection` 要素に追加すると、フィルタされたコレクションでも標準の ObjectId を使用できます（APAR PJ45541）。  
   ```xml
   <tns:Collection … idType="ObjectID">
   ```

5. **アクセス制御の設定**  
   - **z/TPF ユーザーセキュリティ DB**：フィルタされたコレクションに対するロールを作成し、ユーザーに割り当てる。  
   - **MongoDB フィルタコレクションアクセス制御ユーザーエグジット（UATH_filteredCollection）**：レコード単位で細かく制御したい場合に使用。

6. **サポートされる操作**  
   フィルタされたコレクションでは `find()`, `findOne()`, `update()` が利用可能です。`insert()` と `remove()` はサポートされません。

**まとめ**  
- コレクション記述子で `filtered="true"` を設定し、必要な LREC と（必要なら）`<FilterRule>` を記述する。  
- アクセス権は z/TPF ユーザーセキュリティ DB か、MongoDB のユーザーエグジットで管理する。  
- `_id` の形式は `idType` 属性で選択でき、操作は `find` 系と `update` に限定されます。

 Use the DBRC keyword to request or bypass the database recovery control (DBRC) facility process for the database that is specified by the DBD. 
 Processing includes DBRC sign-on and sign-off, area authorization, and event notification. To process multiple area data sets (MADS), DBRC=YES must be specified.   
 If you specify DBRC=YES for the CHANGE, the INITIALIZE, or the RELOAD command, the RECOV NEEDED status of the area is changed to OFF for that command. 
 If you specify DBRC=YES for the INDEXBLD command with the IDXPROC=BUILD option, FPA issues the NOTIFY.REORG command to DBRC only for the secondary index databases that were built successfully. 
 If you specify ICOUT DD, DBRC=YES, and ICNOTIFY=YES, FPA issues the NOTIFY.IC command to DBRC. This option is valid for the following commands:   ANALYZE

Content: IMS 15.6 - System administration - Considerations for a DBRC system
Considerations for a DBRC system   
 DBRC controls database-related and log-related processes. 
   These processes include: 
   Creating backup copies of databases 
 Creating DB change accumulation data sets 
 Recovering databases 
 Protecting databases that need backout 
 Archiving OLDSs 
           
 General considerations for using DBRC  DBRC has several considerations to be aware of during it's use.  
 
 Data set naming conventions  In most cases, the use of z/OS® catalog facilities for image copy and change accumulation data sets is optional because DBRC always records volume serial information pertaining to these data sets in the RECON data set. If you catalog image copy and change accumulation data sets, they must have unique data set names. 
 
 Database backup copies  When IMS takes a regular system checkpoint, it records internal control information for DL/I (for Fast Path, IMS also records buffers and MSDBs), but it does not record the external contents of the database. If the database is lost, examining the last system checkpoint does not help. The log can tell you what changes have occurred, but without a backup copy of the database, recovery is impossible. 
 
 Log record change accumulation  As IMS runs, the number of stored SLDSs or RLDSs grows. You can use these stored volumes to recover a lost or damaged database, but to use them in their raw form would be inefficient. 
 
 DBDS group considerations  A DBDS group is a named collection of DBDSs or DEDB areas. DBRC can perform various operations by DBDS group so that you do not need to repeat the command for every member of the group.

Content: IMS 15.6 - System administration - Overview of DBRC
Overview of DBRC   
 A feature of the IMS Database Manager that facilitates easier recovery of IMS databases, DBRC maintains information that is required for database recoveries, generates recovery control statements, verifies recovery input, maintains a separate change log for database data sets, and supports sharing of IMS databases and areas by multiple IMS subsystems. 
 DBRC is an integral part of IMS. IMS relies on DBRC to record and manage information about many items. DBRC keeps this information in a set of VSAM data sets that are collectively called the recovery control (RECON) data set and advises IMS (based on the information in the RECON data set) about how to proceed. 
 Specifically, DBRC: 
   Helps you ensure IMS system and database integrity by recording and managing information associated with the logging process. 
 Assists IMS in the restart process by notifying IMS which logs to use for restart. 
 Assists IMS to allow or prevent access to databases in data-sharing environments by recording and managing database authorization information. 
 Facilitates database and log recovery by:    Controlling the use and integrity of the information in the logs. 
 Recording and maintaining information about the databases and logs in the RECON data set. 
 Generating and verifying the Job Control Language (JCL) for various IMS utility programs. 
   
 Supports Extended Recovery Facility (XRF) by identifying (in the RECON data set) if the subsystem is XRF capable. 
 Supports IMSplexes by:    Notifying all DBRCs in the same IMSplex within the same DBRC sharing group when one of the DBRCs performs a RECON data set reconfiguration. 
 Allowing parallel access to the RECON data set. 
   
   DBRC also plays a key role in managing the log data needed to restart and recover IMS online subsystems. 
 Most IMS configurations require DBRC, including:    
   Online configurations: DB/DC, DCCTL, or DBCTL 
 Data-sharing environments, including IMSplexes

Content: Data format conversions   
  When the code in your program involves the interaction of items that have different data formats, the compiler converts those items either temporarily, for comparisons and arithmetic operations, or  permanently, for assignment to the receiver in a  MOVE  or  COMPUTE  statement .  
 A conversion is actually a move of a value from one data item to another. The compiler performs any conversions that are required during the execution of arithmetic or comparisons by using the same rules that are used for  MOVE  and  COMPUTE  statements. 
 When possible, the compiler performs a move to preserve numeric value instead of a direct digit-for-digit move. 
 
 Conversion generally requires additional storage and processing time because data is moved to an internal work area and converted before the operation is performed. The results might also have to be moved back into a work area and converted again. 
 
  Conversions between fixed-point data formats (external decimal, packed decimal, or binary) are without loss of precision provided that the target field can contain all the digits of the source operand. 
 
  A loss of precision is possible in conversions between fixed-point data formats and floating-point data formats (short floating point, long floating point, or external floating point). These conversions happen during arithmetic evaluations that have a mixture of both fixed-point and floating-point operands. 
 
 
 Related references       Conversions and precision      Sign representation of zoned and packed-decimal data       
       
 Conversions and precision   In some numeric conversions, a loss of precision is possible; other conversions preserve precision or result in rounding.

URL: 
Score: 0.20743978023529053
Content: z/TPF  utilization impact     The following list contains items in  z/TPF  that can affect  z/TPF  processor utilization when using  z/TPFAR .  All users need to evaluate their own requirements for utilization and  z/TPFAR  in order to adjust their system accordingly.     The format of the data type.  When the table is created on  Db2® , information about the column types is supplied. When a user program asks for the data back in a different form (for instance the table column was created as a floating point number, but the application wants the data in an integer format), this causes additional  z/TPF  overhead to convert the data to the requested type. 
 
 The number of affected columns.   The larger the number of columns returned on an SQL SELECT or the larger the number of columns used on an SQL INSERT, the more the processing time is affected. The affected columns can have a large impact on processing time, especially on SQL SELECTS. With SQL, you can specify the specific columns that you want returned to your application.  An application program that issues an SQL SELECT should only request the data that is required for the application. This way, the amount of processing to return a row to the application can be reduced. 
 
 The cumulative size of host variables.   TPF/APPC  limits the size of an RU.  This limit affects the number of host variables that can fit in a single RU. See  Request unit size considerations  for more on the effect this limit has on the system.  TCP/IP  similarly limits the size of a send message. 
 
 The select conditions specified.  When a large number of host variables are used in the condition statement of an SQL command, these variables need to be transmitted to  Db2 . The more host variables there are on a condition statement, the larger the utilization impact on  z/TPF .
z/TPF utilization impact
The SNA pacing for LU 6.2.   When sending a large amount of SQL traffic over SNA, SNA pacing limits need to be evaluated. If the pacing value is too low, the processing of a pacing request or response slows system performance. SNA pacing includes session as well as virtual route (with PU 5 support) pacing. 
 
 The SQL command mix.  Of all the SQL commands, the cursor-related, blocked-SQL fetch especially affects system performance. When using the blocked-SQL fetch, multiple rows of the answer set are sent back to  z/TPF  from  Db2 . When the application requests the next row,  z/TPF  can use the row information already returned by  Db2 , rather then having to go back to  Db2 . 
 
 Run-time binding versus static binding.   Run-time binding can be a convenient method for managing DBRMs across multiple platforms.  Run-time binding incurs the overhead of the time required to perform the bind.  This overhead depends on the system load and configuration. Once a DBRM is bound for a given program on a  Db2  system, there is no performance difference between run-time binding and static binding.
